To form the passive voice: ser + participle (agreeing) + por.
To use the passive with “se”: se venden casas, se construyó un puente.
To use impersonal “se”: se dice que, se vive bien, se come tarde.
To choose the right form: in spoken Spanish, “se” is much more common than “ser + participle”.
To describe a city and its history like a tour guide.
September. Carmen, Ana’s mother, has come to Bucharest to see her pregnant daughter. Mihai takes her to see the city. First stop: the Palace of the Parliament.
Good heavens! What’s this enormous building?
It’s the Palace of the Parliament. It was built in the eighties, during Ceaușescu’s dictatorship.
It was designed by a very young architect, Anca Petrescu. She was only twenty-eight.
Incredible. People say it’s very big, but I didn’t imagine it was this big.
It’s the second-largest administrative building in the world, after the Pentagon. And it’s believed to be the heaviest.
A whole neighbourhood. To build it, thousands of houses, churches and a hospital were knocked down. Many people were forced to leave their homes.
How sad… Can it be visited?
Yes, guided tours are organised. But you need your passport to get in, and photos are forbidden in some rooms.
Well, my passport is at the hotel. What else is there to see in Bucharest?
The historic centre. Eighteenth-century churches and very pretty streets have been preserved there. And the food is very good.
The food’s good? That interests me more than the palace. What time do people eat here?
Much earlier than in Spain. Here people have lunch at one and dinner at seven.
At seven? At that time in Madrid we’re having our afternoon snack! Oh well, when you travel, you adapt.
That’s the spirit. Come on, let’s go to the centre before the restaurants fill up.

In the passive, the participle agrees: construido (el palacio), construida (la casa), construidos, construidas. Listen to the ending: -DO, -DA, -DOS, -DAS.
SEE-glo: a soft “g” before the “l”. Centuries are read with cardinal numbers: el siglo dieciocho (not “decimoctavo”).
Spaniards say “chow-SES-koo”. Spanish has no ș or ă sounds, so they approximate.
1. The passive with SER: ser + participle + por
As in English (“was built by…”), Spanish has a passive with the verb SER + participle. The participle AGREES with the subject in gender and number.
El palacio fue diseñado por Anca Petrescu.
El Quijote fue escrito por Cervantes.
The tense is shown by SER: es construido (present), fue construido (indefinido), ha sido construido (perfect), será construido (future).

This passive appears mainly in written texts: newspapers, history, tourist guides. In conversation, Spaniards prefer the passive with “se” (point 2) or the active. English uses the passive much more than Spanish does!
2. The passive with SE: se venden pisos
The most common passive in Spanish: SE + verb in the third person. The verb agrees with the thing we’re talking about (singular or plural):
Where English says “Flat for sale”, “Rooms to let” or “Two bridges were built”, Spanish simply says se + verb. Short and very common!
With the “se” passive you DON’T say who does the action. “Se construyó por el Gobierno” is wrong. If you want to say who, use ser + participle + por.
3. Impersonal SE: se dice que, se vive bien
When you talk about people in general (with no particular subject), use SE + verb in the third person SINGULAR — like English “people…”, “you…” or “one…”:
In Romania people have dinner at seven.
How do you say “gracias” in Romanian?
Very useful expressions: se dice que (people say), se cree que (it’s believed), se sabe que (it’s known), se puede (you can), no se puede (you can’t), se necesita (you need).
With reflexive verbs (adaptarse, levantarse) you can’t use impersonal “se” (it would be “se se adapta”). Then use “uno/una”: Cuando se viaja, uno se adapta. Carmen says “una” because she’s a woman.

Carmen picked up a brochure for Spanish tourists at the hotel. Here it is.
One. According to legend, Bucharest was founded by a shepherd called Bucur. His name has been preserved in the little Bucur Church, by the river.
Two. At the beginning of the 20th century, the city was called “Little Paris”, because its boulevards and buildings were inspired by the French capital.
Three. There’s also an Arc de Triomphe here. It was built in 1936 and is a little smaller than the one in Paris.
Four. In December 1989, the dictatorship was overthrown by a revolution. Bullet holes can still be seen on some façades in the centre.

On the last day of her visit, Carmen wanted to see something that wasn’t in the guidebooks. She asked Mihai to take her to the neighbourhood where his mother, Elena, had grown up.
It was a neighbourhood of low houses, with yards full of vines and cats asleep on the walls. Many houses were abandoned. On some doors you could read old signs: “For sale.” “To let.”
“My grandmother lived here,” said Mihai, stopping in front of a yellow house with boarded-up windows. “My mother was born in this house.”
Carmen looked at the house in silence. You could tell it had been beautiful. It had a wrought-iron balcony with flowers and a wooden door with a knocker shaped like a hand.
“In the eighties, this neighbourhood was going to be knocked down, like the one where the palace is now. The families were told they had to leave. My grandmother refused.”
“The revolution came. The plan was cancelled. The neighbourhood was saved at the last minute. But my grandmother died soon afterwards, and the house was left empty. Nobody wanted to live here.”
At that moment the door of the house next door opened. A very old lady came out, with a black headscarf and a walking stick. She looked at Mihai with narrowed eyes.
She said something in Romanian. Mihai froze. Then he answered, in a shaky voice. The lady came closer slowly and touched his face with her hand, as if she wanted to check he was real.
“She says I’m the spitting image of my grandfather. Her name is Mrs Maria. She was my grandmother’s best friend. She says she has something for me. She’s kept it for thirty-five years.”

Mrs Maria’s house smelled of quince and wax. There were icons on every wall and a green tiled stove in one corner. She served them cherry preserve on little crystal plates and a glass of cold water, the way guests are treated in Romania.
Then she opened a chest and took out a rusty metal box. Inside were photos, letters and a big iron key.

“It’s the key to the house,” Mihai translated. “My grandmother gave it to her before she died. She told her: ‘Keep it until someone from the family comes back. And tell them this house was saved for a reason.’”
Mihai held the key in his hands. It was much heavier than it looked.
Among the photos there was one of a young woman sitting on the iron balcony with a little girl in her arms. On the back was written: “Elena, 1962”.
“It’s my mother,” said Mihai. “As a baby.”
Carmen put her hand on his shoulder. There was no need to say anything.
That evening, in the flat, Mihai showed Ana the key. He told her the whole story. Ana listened with her hands on her belly.
“And what are you going to do with it?” Ana asked.
“I don’t know. The house is in a very bad state. It would need to be almost completely restored. It would cost a lot of money.”
Carmen, who was sitting on the sofa with a cup of tea, looked up.
“Mihai, in Madrid we say that houses have a memory too. That they remember who lived in them. If that house was saved once, maybe it was so that you two could save it again.”
For a while nobody said anything. On the wall, Andrei’s drawings seemed to be looking at them. Grandpa Gheorghe’s cradle gleamed by the window.
“A house with a yard,” Ana said slowly. “So Rosa Elena can play outside. With vines and cats.”
“And a neighbour who makes the best cherry preserve in Bucharest,” added Carmen.
Mihai looked at the key. Then at the two women. And for the first time in a long while, he felt that something that had been lost was about to be found again.

The next day, before Carmen left for the airport, the three of them went back to the neighbourhood. Mihai put the key in the lock. It was stiff and rusty. But after a few seconds, with a long, deep sound, it turned.
The door creaked open. Inside it smelled of dust and old wood. Light came in through the cracks in the windows and drew golden stripes on the floor.

In the middle of the empty living room, on a chair, stood a vase of dried flowers. Mrs Maria, from the doorway, said something softly. “She says she’s changed them every spring since my grandmother died,” Mihai translated. “So the house wouldn’t feel lonely.”
